sourceNote: Hand-authored exam-style scenarios. Every situation, option and rationale was written from AWS's published service documentation, service FAQs and the Well-Architected Framework. None of this is derived from reported live exam questions — see the no-exam-dumps rule in README.md. The point of this bank is the shape the real exam uses: a situation, competing constraints, and distractors that are nearly right but violate one of them.
authoringRules: Every scenario states at least one hard constraint the wrong answers violate (time, cost, durability, operational overhead, compliance).
Distractors must be plausible. A distractor nobody would pick teaches nothing.
Every option carries a `why` — the wrong ones explain which constraint they break, not just 'this is wrong'.
`teaches` lists entity ids so a missed scenario feeds weak spots and spaced repetition.
One clearly best answer. If two options both satisfy every constraint, the scenario is broken.

scenarios.situation: A company runs its application on Amazon EC2 instances and stores data in Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. An auditor asks who is responsible for applying operating system security patches to each tier.
scenarios.question: Under the AWS shared responsibility model, who patches the operating systems?

options.text: AWS patches both the EC2 operating system and the RDS operating system
options.why: AWS never patches the guest operating system on EC2. That instance is yours to maintain — this is the single most common misreading of the model.

options.text: The customer patches both the EC2 operating system and the RDS operating system
options.why: RDS is a managed service. You have no operating system access to patch, and AWS handles it during your maintenance window.

options.text: The customer patches the EC2 operating system; AWS patches the RDS operating system
options.why: The boundary moves with the service. EC2 gives you the OS, so you own it. RDS abstracts the OS away, so AWS owns it. You still own your data and access control in both.

options.text: AWS patches the EC2 operating system; the customer patches the RDS operating system
options.why: Exactly backwards. You cannot even reach the RDS operating system, and AWS deliberately does not touch your EC2 guest OS.

scenarios.situation: A company is moving a production workload to AWS. They need 24/7 phone access to Cloud Support Engineers and a designated Technical Account Manager who knows their environment.
scenarios.question: Which AWS Support plan is the lowest tier that meets both requirements?

options.text: Developer
options.why: Business-hours email access to Cloud Support Associates only. No phone, no TAM.

options.text: Business
options.why: Does give 24/7 phone, chat and email access — but no Technical Account Manager. This is the classic near-miss on this question.

options.text: Enterprise On-Ramp
options.why: The lowest tier with both: 24/7 access to Cloud Support Engineers and a TAM, though the TAM is pooled rather than designated.

options.text: Basic
options.why: Covers billing and account questions plus service health only. No technical support at all.

scenarios.situation: A company has run the same fleet of EC2 instances continuously for two years and expects to keep running them for at least three more. They are currently paying On-Demand rates and want to cut the bill without changing the architecture.
scenarios.question: Which purchasing option best reduces cost?

options.text: Move the fleet to Spot Instances
options.why: Cheapest per hour, but AWS can reclaim Spot capacity with two minutes' notice. Unacceptable for a steady production fleet.

options.text: Commit to a three-year Compute Savings Plan
options.why: Steady, predictable, long-running usage is exactly what a commitment discount is for, and a Compute Savings Plan still allows changes of instance family and Region.

options.text: Keep On-Demand but enable Auto Scaling
options.why: Auto Scaling helps when load varies. This load does not vary — you would still pay full On-Demand rates for the same steady capacity.

options.text: Move the fleet to Dedicated Hosts
options.why: Dedicated Hosts cost more, not less. They exist for licence compliance and physical isolation.

scenarios.situation: An external auditor asks the company to provide AWS's current SOC 2 Type II report as evidence that the underlying cloud infrastructure is independently audited.
scenarios.question: Where should the company obtain this report?

options.text: AWS Artifact
options.why: Artifact is the self-service portal for AWS's own audit reports and agreements. This is exactly what it exists for.

options.text: AWS Config
options.why: Config records how your resources are configured and whether they match your rules. It says nothing about AWS's own certifications.

options.text: AWS Security Hub
options.why: Aggregates security findings about your account against best-practice standards. It does not supply AWS's audit reports.

options.text: Open a support case with AWS Support
options.why: Unnecessary — the documents are available immediately in Artifact without waiting on a case.

scenarios.situation: A finance team wants an email as soon as it looks likely that this month's AWS spend will exceed £5,000 — ideally before the money has actually been spent.
scenarios.question: Which service meets this requirement?

options.text: AWS Cost Explorer
options.why: Excellent for analysing and forecasting spend visually, but it does not send alerts. Someone has to go and look.

options.text: AWS Budgets
options.why: Budgets alerts on both actual and *forecast* spend. The forecast alarm is the part that gives you time to react before the money is gone.

options.text: AWS Cost and Usage Report
options.why: Delivers detailed line-item billing data to S3 for analysis. No alerting of its own.

options.text: Amazon CloudWatch billing metrics with no alarm configured
options.why: The metric alone notifies nobody. Without an alarm and an SNS topic, nothing is sent.

scenarios.situation: A new cloud team has inherited an AWS account that has grown organically for three years. They suspect there are idle resources, security groups open to the world, and service limits close to being hit.
scenarios.question: Which service gives them a single review covering all three concerns?

options.text: AWS Trusted Advisor
options.why: Trusted Advisor checks span cost optimisation, security, fault tolerance, performance and service limits — the exact three areas named.

options.text: Amazon Inspector
options.why: Finds software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure. It says nothing about idle spend or service quotas.

options.text: AWS Compute Optimizer
options.why: Right-sizes compute from real utilisation. Useful for the idle resources, but covers neither security groups nor quotas.

options.text: AWS Cost Explorer
options.why: Cost only, and it reports spend rather than flagging idle resources as findings.

scenarios.situation: A media company keeps 40 TB of finished video renders in Amazon S3 Standard. After the first 30 days a file is almost never requested, but when a client does request one it must be retrievable within minutes. Storage cost is the primary concern.
scenarios.question: Which approach meets the requirements at the lowest storage cost?

options.text: A lifecycle rule moving objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days
options.why: The cheapest storage of all, but standard retrieval takes up to 12 hours. That breaks the 'within minutes' requirement outright.

options.text: A lifecycle rule moving objects to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 30 days
options.why: Far cheaper than Standard, and Expedited retrieval returns objects in minutes. The lifecycle rule automates the transition at exactly the 30-day mark described.

options.text: A lifecycle rule moving objects to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days
options.why: Retrieval is immediate, which satisfies the time constraint, but Standard-IA costs considerably more per GB than Glacier. The question asks for lowest cost.

options.text: Leave objects in S3 Standard and enable S3 Versioning
options.why: Changes nothing about cost, and versioning increases storage by keeping old copies.

scenarios.situation: A content management application runs on a fleet of Linux EC2 instances behind a load balancer, spread across three Availability Zones. Every instance must read and write the same set of uploaded files, and the fleet scales up and down through the day.
scenarios.question: Which storage option meets the requirement?

options.text: Attach a single Amazon EBS volume to all instances
options.why: An EBS volume lives in one Availability Zone, and even Multi-Attach is limited to instances in that same AZ. It cannot serve a three-AZ fleet.

options.text: Use Amazon EFS mounted on every instance
options.why: EFS is a regional NFS file system with mount targets in each AZ, shared concurrently by many Linux instances, and it grows and shrinks automatically as the fleet does.

options.text: Use Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
options.why: FSx for Windows speaks SMB and targets Windows workloads. These are Linux instances, and SMB is the wrong protocol here.

options.text: Copy files to each instance's instance store at launch
options.why: Instance store is ephemeral and local to one instance. Writes on one machine would be invisible to the others and lost on stop.

scenarios.situation: An online shop's web tier writes orders directly to a backend processing service. During flash sales the web tier accepts orders far faster than the backend can process them, and orders are being lost when the backend becomes overwhelmed.
scenarios.question: Which change best prevents order loss during traffic spikes?

options.text: Place orders on an Amazon SQS queue that the backend polls at its own rate
options.why: The queue absorbs the burst and holds each order durably until processed. If a consumer crashes mid-order the message reappears after the visibility timeout rather than being lost.

options.text: Publish orders to an Amazon SNS topic the backend subscribes to
options.why: SNS pushes immediately and does not store messages waiting for a slow consumer. An overwhelmed backend would still drop work — this is the most tempting wrong answer.

options.text: Scale the backend vertically to a larger instance type
options.why: Raises the ceiling but does not remove it, requires downtime to resize, and leaves you paying for peak capacity all the time.

options.text: Add retry logic with exponential backoff in the web tier
options.why: Helps with transient errors, but the web tier still has to hold the order in memory while retrying. A web-tier restart loses it.

scenarios.situation: A team runs Amazon RDS for MySQL. They have two separate goals: the database must survive the loss of an Availability Zone with automatic failover, and a growing reporting workload is slowing down the primary.
scenarios.question: Which combination addresses both goals?

options.text: Enable Multi-AZ only
options.why: Solves the failover goal, but the standby cannot be read from. Reporting queries would still hit the primary.

options.text: Add read replicas only
options.why: Solves the reporting goal, but replicas are asynchronous and are not an automatic failover mechanism.

options.text: Enable Multi-AZ and add one or more read replicas
options.why: The two features solve different problems and are designed to be used together: Multi-AZ for automatic failover, read replicas for scaling reads away from the primary.

options.text: Enable Multi-AZ and direct reporting queries to the standby
options.why: The Multi-AZ standby is not readable. This is the single most common misconception about RDS.

scenarios.situation: EC2 instances in a private subnet need to read objects from an Amazon S3 bucket in the same Region. Security requires that this traffic never traverses the public internet, and the team wants to avoid unnecessary data-processing charges.
scenarios.question: What should the architect implement?

options.text: A NAT gateway in a public subnet with a route for S3 traffic
options.why: Works, but the traffic leaves your VPC toward the public S3 endpoint, and NAT gateways charge hourly plus per GB processed. It fails both stated requirements.

options.text: A gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3
options.why: Gateway endpoints keep S3 traffic inside the AWS network via a route-table entry, and they carry no hourly or per-GB charge at all.

options.text: An interface VPC endpoint for Amazon S3
options.why: Also keeps traffic private and does work — but interface endpoints bill per hour and per GB. For S3 in the same Region the gateway endpoint is the cheaper, purpose-built answer.

options.text: An internet gateway with a restrictive security group
options.why: An internet gateway makes the subnet public by definition, which contradicts the requirement that traffic stay off the internet.

scenarios.situation: A web application stores user session data in memory on each EC2 instance. When Auto Scaling removes an instance, those users are logged out and lose their shopping baskets.
scenarios.question: Which change resolves this most effectively?

options.text: Enable sticky sessions on the Application Load Balancer
options.why: Pins a user to one instance, so the problem returns the moment that instance is replaced — and it undermines even load distribution. A workaround, not a fix.

options.text: Store session data in Amazon ElastiCache or Amazon DynamoDB
options.why: Moving state off the instance makes the tier genuinely stateless: any instance can serve any request, and instances can be added or destroyed freely.

options.text: Store session data on an Amazon EBS volume attached to each instance
options.why: The volume is still tied to a single instance and is deleted with it by default. Same failure, different storage.

options.text: Disable Auto Scaling so instances are never removed
options.why: Removes elasticity and does not help when an instance fails on its own, which it eventually will.

scenarios.situation: A research team runs nightly image-processing jobs. Each job takes about 90 minutes, jobs are independent, and a job that is interrupted can simply be re-run. The team wants the lowest possible compute cost.
scenarios.question: Which purchasing option should they use?

options.text: Spot Instances
options.why: The deepest discount available, and the workload has exactly the property Spot requires: interruption is harmless because the job can be re-run.

options.text: On-Demand Instances
options.why: No interruption risk, but the most expensive per hour — and the workload does not need that guarantee.

options.text: Reserved Instances
options.why: Commitment discounts suit steady, always-on usage. A nightly batch leaves the reservation idle most of the day.

options.text: Dedicated Hosts
options.why: The most expensive option, intended for licence compliance and physical isolation. Neither applies here.

scenarios.situation: A company must move 500 TB of archival data from an on-premises data centre into Amazon S3. The site has a 100 Mbps internet connection that is also used by staff, and the migration should complete within a few weeks.
scenarios.question: What is the most appropriate transfer method?

options.text: AWS DataSync over the existing internet connection
options.why: At 100 Mbps, 500 TB would take well over a year even with the line fully saturated — which would also cripple staff connectivity.

options.text: AWS Snowball devices
options.why: When the network would take longer than shipping physical media, Snow is the answer. Data is encrypted on tamper-evident devices and posted, bypassing the constrained line entirely.

options.text: Order AWS Direct Connect and transfer over the dedicated link
options.why: Provisioning Direct Connect commonly takes weeks to months before a single byte moves, and the circuit is an ongoing cost for a one-off migration.

options.text: Upload directly with the AWS CLI using multipart upload
options.why: Multipart improves reliability and parallelism but cannot exceed the 100 Mbps physical limit.

scenarios.situation: An application on EC2 needs to read objects from one specific S3 bucket. A developer has hard-coded their own IAM user's access keys into the application configuration file.
scenarios.question: What should the architect do instead?

options.text: Attach an IAM role to the EC2 instance granting read access to that bucket only
options.why: Roles supply temporary, automatically rotated credentials that never sit in a config file, scoped to exactly the access needed. This is the textbook answer.

options.text: Create a dedicated IAM user for the application and store its keys in the config file
options.why: Better scoped, but long-lived keys in a file are still the leak everyone worries about, and they do not rotate on their own.

options.text: Store the developer's access keys in AWS Secrets Manager and fetch them at runtime
options.why: An improvement on plaintext, but the application still needs credentials to reach Secrets Manager — and a human's personal keys should never back an application in the first place.

options.text: Make the S3 bucket public so no credentials are required
options.why: Exposes the data to the entire internet to avoid a credential problem. Never the answer.

scenarios.situation: A company hosts a marketing website consisting entirely of static HTML, CSS, images and JavaScript. Visitors are spread worldwide and complain that the site is slow outside Europe. The team wants minimal operational overhead and low cost.
scenarios.question: Which architecture best meets the requirements?

options.text: Host the files in Amazon S3 and serve them through Amazon CloudFront
options.why: No servers to manage, and CloudFront caches at edge locations worldwide so distant visitors are served locally. Egress through CloudFront is also cheaper than straight from S3.

options.text: Run EC2 web servers behind an Application Load Balancer in one Region
options.why: Servers to patch and scale, and every request still crosses the world to that single Region. Highest cost, highest overhead, does not fix latency.

options.text: Host the files in Amazon S3 with public read access and no CDN
options.why: Removes the servers but not the distance. Requests from other continents still travel to the bucket's Region.

options.text: Deploy EC2 web servers in six Regions with Route 53 latency routing
options.why: Would improve latency, but at six times the fleet management and cost for content that is entirely static.

scenarios.situation: A public web application behind Amazon CloudFront is receiving SQL injection attempts and requests from a handful of IP addresses making thousands of requests per minute.
scenarios.question: Which service should be used to block this traffic?

options.text: AWS WAF attached to the CloudFront distribution
options.why: WAF inspects HTTP(S) requests at the application layer: managed rule groups cover SQL injection, and rate-based rules throttle abusive IPs. Attaching at CloudFront stops it at the edge.

options.text: AWS Shield Standard
options.why: Already enabled for every customer and aimed at volumetric network-layer floods. It does not inspect request content for injection patterns.

options.text: Network ACLs on the VPC subnets
options.why: Operate at layer 4 on IP and port. They cannot see an SQL injection string inside an HTTP request body.

options.text: Security groups on the origin instances
options.why: Stateful allow-only firewalls attached to resources. They cannot deny specific addresses, nor inspect request content.

scenarios.situation: A business-critical application must be recoverable in another AWS Region. The business states a recovery point objective of five minutes and a recovery time objective of thirty minutes. Cost should be kept as low as the objectives allow.
scenarios.question: Which disaster recovery strategy is most appropriate?

options.text: Backup and restore
options.why: The cheapest strategy, but restoring infrastructure and data from backups takes hours. It cannot meet a thirty-minute RTO.

options.text: Pilot light
options.why: Keeps data replicated with core services switched off. Closer, but scaling the environment up from nothing typically exceeds thirty minutes.

options.text: Warm standby
options.why: A scaled-down but running copy in the second Region with continuous replication. Data is minutes behind, and scaling an already-running environment fits a thirty-minute RTO — without the cost of full active/active.

options.text: Multi-site active/active
options.why: Would comfortably beat both objectives, but runs full production capacity in two Regions. The question explicitly asks for the lowest cost that still meets the targets.

scenarios.situation: A multiplayer game server communicates with clients over UDP. Players worldwide report inconsistent latency, and the studio also needs fixed IP addresses that can be embedded in the game client, plus fast failover between Regions.
scenarios.question: Which service should the architect use?

options.text: Amazon CloudFront
options.why: A content delivery network built around caching HTTP(S) content. It does not carry UDP game traffic, and there is nothing cacheable here.

options.text: AWS Global Accelerator
options.why: Provides static anycast IP addresses, moves TCP and UDP traffic onto the AWS backbone at the nearest edge, and fails over between regional endpoints quickly. Purpose-built for this case.

options.text: Amazon Route 53 with latency-based routing
options.why: Improves endpoint selection, but DNS answers are cached by clients and resolvers, so failover is slow — and it provides no static IPs.

options.text: An Application Load Balancer in each Region
options.why: ALBs handle HTTP(S) only and cannot balance UDP. A Network Load Balancer could, but that alone gives no global routing.

scenarios.situation: A compliance review finds an existing production EBS volume was created without encryption. The data must be encrypted at rest, and the team wants the shortest possible maintenance window.
scenarios.question: What is the correct procedure?

options.text: Enable encryption on the existing volume in the console
options.why: There is no such toggle. Encryption is set when a volume is created and cannot be turned on in place — this is the whole reason the question exists.

options.text: Take a snapshot, copy the snapshot with encryption enabled, create a new volume from the encrypted copy and attach it
options.why: The supported path. The snapshot copy operation is where encryption gets applied, and the only downtime is detaching the old volume and attaching the new one.

options.text: Create an encrypted volume and change the instance's root device mapping to point at it
options.why: Produces an empty encrypted volume. The existing data is never copied across.

options.text: Enable default EBS encryption for the Region
options.why: An excellent control going forward, but it applies only to newly created volumes. The existing one stays unencrypted.

scenarios.situation: A product catalogue in Amazon DynamoDB serves a very high volume of repeated reads for the same popular items. Response times of single-digit milliseconds are no longer fast enough, and the team wants microsecond reads without rewriting the application's DynamoDB API calls.
scenarios.question: What should be added?

options.text: Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)
options.why: A DynamoDB-native in-memory cache delivering microsecond reads, and it is API-compatible — the application keeps making the same calls.

options.text: Amazon ElastiCache for Redis in front of the table
options.why: Would deliver the speed, but the application must be rewritten to check the cache, handle misses and manage invalidation. The question rules that out.

options.text: Increase the table's provisioned read capacity
options.why: Removes throttling if that were the issue, but does not reduce per-request latency below DynamoDB's single-digit milliseconds.

options.text: Add a global secondary index on the popular items
options.why: Indexes change how you can query, not how fast an already-fast key lookup returns.

scenarios.situation: A company runs 40 AWS accounts under AWS Organizations. Security needs an immutable record of every API call in every account, stored centrally, including any accounts created in future.
scenarios.question: What should be configured?

options.text: An organization trail in AWS CloudTrail delivering to a central S3 bucket
options.why: An organization trail applies to every member account automatically, including accounts added later, and delivers to one bucket in a dedicated logging account.

options.text: A separate CloudTrail trail in each account delivering to that account's own bucket
options.why: Logs stay scattered, and every new account needs manual setup that will eventually be forgotten.

options.text: Enable AWS Config in every account with an aggregator
options.why: Config records resource configuration state and compliance, not the API calls that changed it. Wrong tool for an audit trail of actions.

options.text: Rely on CloudTrail Event history in each account
options.why: Event history keeps only the last 90 days, is not centralised, and cannot be made immutable.

scenarios.situation: An order pipeline runs five AWS Lambda functions in sequence. Each function invokes the next directly. When a middle step fails intermittently the team cannot tell which order failed at which step, and the retry logic has been copied into every function.
scenarios.question: Which change best addresses both problems?

options.text: Orchestrate the five functions with AWS Step Functions
options.why: Retry and catch behaviour is declared per state instead of duplicated in code, and each execution is visible step by step so a failure is immediately attributable.

options.text: Put an SQS queue between each pair of functions
options.why: Improves durability between steps, but you still have no single view of one order's journey, and the retry code stays scattered.

options.text: Increase each function's timeout and memory
options.why: Addresses neither visibility nor duplicated retry logic. It only masks slow steps.

options.text: Combine all five functions into one larger function
options.why: Makes failures harder to isolate, not easier, and risks hitting the 15-minute Lambda limit.

scenarios.situation: A financial services regulator requires that encryption keys be held in single-tenant, FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated hardware that the cloud provider cannot access, and the customer must control the entire key lifecycle.
scenarios.question: Which service satisfies the requirement?

options.text: AWS KMS with a customer managed key
options.why: You control policy and rotation, but the underlying HSM fleet is multi-tenant and operated by AWS. It does not meet a single-tenant requirement.

options.text: AWS CloudHSM
options.why: Dedicated single-tenant HSMs that only you can access — AWS cannot recover your keys, which is precisely the property the regulator is asking for.

options.text: AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation
options.why: Stores and rotates secrets such as passwords. It is not key-storage hardware and has no FIPS Level 3 single-tenant guarantee.

options.text: AWS KMS with an imported key
options.why: Lets you supply key material, but it still resides in AWS's multi-tenant KMS infrastructure.

scenarios.situation: An internal expenses API receives roughly 200 requests per day, clustered around month end and almost nothing in between. It currently runs on two t3.medium EC2 instances behind a load balancer, running 24 hours a day.
scenarios.question: Which change would most reduce cost?

options.text: Re-implement the API on AWS Lambda behind Amazon API Gateway
options.why: With 200 requests a day the compute is idle over 99% of the time. Lambda charges only for actual execution, so the idle cost falls to nothing.

options.text: Move to smaller t3.micro instances
options.why: Cuts the bill somewhat but still pays for two instances running around the clock to serve a handful of requests.

options.text: Purchase Reserved Instances for the two instances
options.why: Discounts capacity that should not be running at all. Committing to three years of waste is not optimisation.

options.text: Add Auto Scaling to the existing fleet
options.why: Auto Scaling has a minimum size, and the load never justifies scaling out. The idle baseline cost remains.

scenarios.situation: A company wants an internal assistant that answers staff questions from its HR policy documents. The policies are revised every few weeks, and answers must be traceable to the document they came from.
scenarios.question: Which approach best meets the requirements?

options.text: Fine-tune a foundation model on the policy documents
options.why: Fine-tuning bakes information into the weights, so every revision means retraining, and the model cannot cite which document an answer came from.

options.text: Use Retrieval Augmented Generation over the policy documents
options.why: Documents are retrieved at question time, so a revision takes effect immediately, and the retrieved passages give you the citation the requirement asks for.

options.text: Paste all policy documents into every prompt
options.why: Would ground the answer, but the documents will exceed the context window, and you would pay for those tokens on every single question.

options.text: Train a model from scratch on the company corpus
options.why: Astronomically expensive, needs far more data than an HR policy set, and still has the staleness and citation problems.

scenarios.situation: A customer-facing assistant built on a foundation model has begun quoting refund terms that do not exist. The wording is confident and reads exactly like the genuine policy.
scenarios.question: What is the most effective first mitigation?

options.text: Lower the temperature setting to zero
options.why: Makes output more deterministic and repetitive, but a model can state a fabricated policy just as consistently. It treats a symptom, not the cause.

options.text: Ground answers in the actual policy documents and require citations
options.why: Hallucination is the model filling gaps from its own weights. Supplying the real text at question time removes the gap, and citations let a reader verify the claim.

options.text: Add "do not make anything up" to the system prompt
options.why: Helps marginally, but the model has no reliable way to know what it does not know. Instructions cannot make it aware of its own gaps.

options.text: Switch to a larger foundation model
options.why: Larger models hallucinate less often, but they still hallucinate, and on a customer-facing refund policy "less often" is not an acceptable control.

scenarios.situation: A bank must demonstrate to a regulator that its loan-approval model does not treat applicants differently by an attribute it is not permitted to use. The model was never given that attribute as an input.
scenarios.question: What should the team do?

options.text: Confirm the attribute is absent from the training data and consider the matter closed
options.why: The common and dangerous assumption. Correlated features — postcode, occupation, purchase history — routinely reconstruct a protected attribute the model never saw directly.

options.text: Measure bias in the data and the model output with SageMaker Clarify
options.why: Clarify measures disparity in outcomes across groups before and after training, which is the evidence a regulator actually wants, and explains which features drove predictions.

options.text: Retrain with a larger dataset
options.why: More data does not remove bias; if the historical data reflects biased decisions, more of it reinforces the pattern.

options.text: Publish the model architecture for transparency
options.why: Architecture says nothing about outcomes. Fairness is measured in results, not in the diagram.

scenarios.situation: A model reaches 99% accuracy on its training data but only 71% on the held-out validation set. The gap has widened with every additional training epoch.
scenarios.question: What is happening, and what is the appropriate response?

options.text: The model is overfitting; add regularisation, more data, or stop training earlier
options.why: A large and widening gap between training and validation accuracy is the definition of overfitting — the model is memorising examples rather than learning the pattern.

options.text: The model is underfitting; train for more epochs with a larger model
options.why: Exactly backwards. Underfitting shows as poor performance on both sets; here training accuracy is excellent.

options.text: The validation set is too small; merge it into the training data
options.why: Removes your only honest measure of generalisation, and gives the model the very data you needed to test it with.

options.text: Tune the learning rate upward to converge faster
options.why: Speeds up convergence toward the same memorised solution. It does not address generalisation.

scenarios.situation: A model performs well in offline evaluation but noticeably worse in production. Investigation shows the feature transformations in the training pipeline and the serving code were written separately and have drifted apart.
scenarios.question: Which approach prevents this class of problem?

options.text: Use SageMaker Feature Store so training and inference read the same feature definitions
options.why: Training/serving skew is exactly what a feature store exists to prevent: one definition, an offline store for training and an online store for serving, guaranteed consistent.

options.text: Retrain the model more frequently
options.why: Retrains on correctly transformed data while serving continues to use different transformations. The mismatch survives.

options.text: Increase the size of the training dataset
options.why: The model is not short of data. It is being shown different inputs at inference than it learned from.

options.text: Deploy the model to a larger instance type
options.why: A performance problem in the accuracy sense, not the latency sense. Hardware changes nothing.

scenarios.situation: A demand-forecasting model deployed nine months ago is producing steadily worse forecasts. The code has not changed and the endpoint is healthy. Buying patterns have shifted since it was trained.
scenarios.question: What should be put in place?

options.text: SageMaker Model Monitor with a baseline from the training data, alarming on drift
options.why: The inputs no longer resemble what the model learned from. Model Monitor compares live traffic against a training baseline and raises the alarm rather than waiting for someone to notice.

options.text: CloudWatch alarms on endpoint latency and error rate
options.why: Operational health is fine — the endpoint answers quickly and without errors. It is the answers that are wrong, which infrastructure metrics cannot see.

options.text: Enable auto scaling on the endpoint
options.why: Addresses load, not accuracy. The model would simply be wrong at greater throughput.

options.text: Roll back to the previous model version
options.why: The older model was trained on even older data, so it fits the current world less well, not more.

scenarios.situation: A retailer scores its entire customer base for churn risk once a night. The job takes about 40 minutes and nothing consumes the predictions until the following morning. A real-time endpoint currently runs continuously to serve it.
scenarios.question: Which change reduces cost without affecting the outcome?

options.text: Switch to SageMaker batch transform
options.why: Batch transform starts, scores the dataset, and shuts down. The endpoint currently bills 24 hours a day to do 40 minutes of work nobody reads until morning.

options.text: Move the endpoint to a smaller instance type
options.why: Reduces the waste rather than removing it, and risks the nightly job no longer finishing in time.

options.text: Switch to serverless inference
options.why: Better than an always-on endpoint, but it is designed for spiky interactive traffic. For one scheduled bulk job, batch transform is both cheaper and simpler.

options.text: Add auto scaling with a minimum of one instance
options.why: That minimum is precisely the idle cost being paid now.

scenarios.situation: A fraud-detection model is evaluated on a dataset where 0.4% of transactions are fraudulent. The model reports 99.6% accuracy. The fraud team says it never catches anything.
scenarios.question: What explains this, and what should be measured instead?

options.text: Accuracy is misleading on imbalanced data; measure recall and precision
options.why: Predicting "not fraud" every time scores 99.6% accuracy while catching nothing. Recall shows how much real fraud is caught, precision how many alerts are genuine.

options.text: The model is overfitting; add regularisation
options.why: Overfitting would show as a training/validation gap. The problem here is that the chosen metric cannot see the failure at all.

options.text: The training set is too small; collect more transactions
options.why: More data at the same ratio produces the same blind spot. The measurement is the problem, not the volume.

options.text: Raise the classification threshold to reduce false positives
options.why: Pushes the model further toward never flagging anything — the opposite of what the fraud team needs.

scenarios.situation: A regulated insurer runs a customer assistant on Amazon Bedrock. It must never discuss competitors or give medical advice, and the team expects to switch to a newer foundation model within the year.
scenarios.question: How should the restrictions be implemented?

options.text: Configure Bedrock Guardrails with denied topics
options.why: Guardrails are configured separately from the model and evaluate both prompt and completion, so the restrictions survive a model swap unchanged.

options.text: Put the restrictions in the system prompt
options.why: Prompts can be argued around by determined users, and every model change means re-tuning the wording. Not an enforcement boundary.

options.text: Fine-tune the model to refuse those topics
options.why: Expensive, imperfect, and thrown away entirely the moment you move to a newer base model — which the team already plans to do.

options.text: Filter the responses with a regular expression before display
options.why: Keyword filtering misses paraphrase and blocks legitimate text. It also cannot catch a medical suggestion phrased in ordinary language.

scenarios.situation: A travel company wants its assistant to do more than answer questions: it should be able to look up a booking, check availability, and cancel a reservation by calling existing internal APIs.
scenarios.question: Which Bedrock capability fits?

options.text: Bedrock Agents with action groups mapped to the internal APIs
options.why: Agents let the model plan which API to call, invoke it, read the result and continue. That is exactly the gap between answering about a booking and changing one.

options.text: Bedrock Knowledge Bases over the booking documentation
options.why: Grounds answers in documents, but retrieval is read-only. It cannot cancel anything.

options.text: A longer system prompt describing the APIs
options.why: Describing an API does not let the model reach it. Something must actually make the call.

options.text: Fine-tune the model on past support transcripts
options.why: Might improve tone and phrasing, but confers no ability to invoke a system.

scenarios.situation: A document-summarisation feature on Bedrock costs far more than forecast. Investigation shows the application sends the entire 80-page document with every request, including for follow-up questions about a single section.
scenarios.question: Which change reduces cost most directly?

options.text: Retrieve and send only the relevant passages for each question
options.why: Billing is per token, and the whole document is being paid for on every request. Retrieval sends the few passages that matter instead of all eighty pages.

options.text: Lower the temperature setting
options.why: Temperature affects how the model chooses words. It has no bearing on how many tokens you send or are billed for.

options.text: Switch to Provisioned Throughput
options.why: Buys reserved capacity at a committed rate. It suits steady high volume, but here the volume itself is the waste.

options.text: Reduce the maximum response length
options.why: Trims output tokens, but the cost is dominated by the eighty pages of input sent every time.

scenarios.situation: A payments service must be released with no downtime, and if a problem appears the team needs to be back on the previous version within seconds rather than minutes.
scenarios.question: Which deployment strategy meets the requirement?

options.text: Blue/green deployment
options.why: The previous environment stays running while traffic moves to the new one, so rollback is a traffic switch measured in seconds rather than a redeploy.

options.text: Rolling deployment
options.why: Avoids downtime, but rolling back means replacing instances again — minutes, not seconds — and both versions serve traffic throughout.

options.text: In-place deployment with a backup AMI
options.why: Cheapest, but rollback means redeploying the old build onto the same instances. Far slower than the requirement allows.

options.text: Canary deployment with a 10% traffic shift
options.why: Excellent for limiting blast radius and often used alongside blue/green — but on its own the old environment is being replaced, so full rollback is not instant.

scenarios.situation: A team deploys a Lambda function several times a day. They want a new version to receive a small share of traffic first, and to roll back automatically if the error rate rises, without anyone watching a dashboard.
scenarios.question: How should this be configured?

options.text: CodeDeploy canary traffic shifting on the Lambda alias with a CloudWatch alarm as the rollback trigger
options.why: CodeDeploy shifts a percentage to the new version and monitors the alarm during the bake period, rolling back automatically if it fires. No human in the loop.

options.text: Publish a new version and update the alias manually after checking metrics
options.why: Works, but requires a person watching, which is exactly what the requirement rules out.

options.text: Use Lambda provisioned concurrency on the new version
options.why: Addresses cold starts. It has nothing to do with traffic shifting or rollback.

options.text: Deploy to a second function and switch the API Gateway integration
options.why: A hand-rolled blue/green with no automatic monitoring or rollback, reimplementing what CodeDeploy already does.

scenarios.situation: A platform team maintains baseline infrastructure across 60 accounts. Engineers occasionally change resources by hand in the console, and the team wants both to deploy the baseline everywhere and to know when an account no longer matches it.
scenarios.question: Which combination addresses both needs?

options.text: CloudFormation StackSets to deploy, and drift detection plus AWS Config rules to spot divergence
options.why: StackSets pushes one template to many accounts and Regions including new ones; drift detection and Config rules report where reality has diverged from the template.

options.text: A separate CloudFormation stack deployed manually in each account
options.why: Sixty manual deployments per change, and nothing watching for hand edits afterwards.

options.text: Service control policies preventing all console access
options.why: Blunt enough to stop legitimate work, and it does not deploy the baseline in the first place.

options.text: AWS Systems Manager Automation runbooks triggered per account
options.why: Good for operational tasks, but it is not a declarative baseline and offers no drift comparison against a desired state.

scenarios.situation: Analysts query two years of clickstream data in Amazon S3 with Athena. Most queries filter to a single day, but the Athena bill is high and queries are slow. The data is stored as uncompressed JSON in one flat prefix.
scenarios.question: Which change reduces both cost and query time most?

options.text: Convert to Parquet and partition by date
options.why: Athena bills per byte scanned. Columnar Parquet reads only the needed columns, and date partitioning means a single-day query touches one partition instead of two years.

options.text: Move the data to S3 Intelligent-Tiering
options.why: Reduces storage cost for infrequently accessed objects. Athena still scans exactly the same bytes at the same price.

options.text: Increase the Athena query timeout
options.why: Lets slow queries run longer. It makes nothing faster or cheaper.

options.text: Load the data into Amazon Redshift
options.why: Would be fast, but introduces a cluster to run and pay for when the existing setup simply needs its file layout fixed.

scenarios.situation: A team must replicate an on-premises Oracle database into Amazon S3 for analytics. The source cannot be taken offline, and the analytics copy should stay within minutes of the source.
scenarios.question: Which approach fits?

options.text: AWS DMS with an initial full load followed by change data capture
options.why: DMS copies the existing data while the source stays online, then streams ongoing changes, which is what keeps the target minutes behind rather than a day.

options.text: A nightly export to CSV uploaded to S3
options.why: Leaves the analytics copy up to 24 hours stale, well outside the stated requirement.

options.text: AWS DataSync scheduled hourly
options.why: DataSync moves files between storage systems. It does not read a live relational database or understand row-level changes.

options.text: AWS Snowball to ship the database
options.why: A one-off bulk transfer with no ongoing replication, and the freshness requirement is continuous.

scenarios.situation: An operations team wants to alarm when memory utilisation on their EC2 instances exceeds 85%. They can see CPU and network metrics in CloudWatch but cannot find a memory metric anywhere.
scenarios.question: Why, and what is needed?

options.text: Memory is inside the guest OS, so the CloudWatch agent must be installed to publish it
options.why: CloudWatch sees the instance from the hypervisor outward. Memory and disk usage live inside the operating system, which is your responsibility, so an agent has to report them.

options.text: Detailed monitoring must be enabled on the instances
options.why: Detailed monitoring raises the frequency of existing metrics from five minutes to one. It does not add new ones.

options.text: The instances need an IAM role granting CloudWatch read access
options.why: A role is needed for the agent to publish, but permissions alone create no metric where nothing is collecting it.

options.text: Memory metrics only appear once an alarm has been created
options.why: Alarms observe metrics that already exist; they never generate them.

scenarios.situation: A compliance requirement states that all EC2 instances must receive operating system security patches within 14 days of release, with evidence of compliance. The fleet spans several accounts and instances have no inbound access from the internet.
scenarios.question: Which service meets this?

options.text: AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager with maintenance windows
options.why: Patch Manager applies a baseline on a schedule and reports compliance per instance. The SSM agent works outbound-only, so no inbound access is needed.

options.text: Amazon Inspector
options.why: Finds and reports vulnerabilities, which is useful evidence — but it does not apply patches.

options.text: A bastion host with a scripted SSH loop
options.why: Reintroduces inbound access the design deliberately avoids, and produces no compliance reporting.

options.text: AWS Config with a managed rule for patch compliance
options.why: Can report on compliance state, but like Inspector it observes rather than remediates.

scenarios.situation: A Lambda function connects to an Amazon RDS database. The password is currently stored in a plaintext environment variable, and security requires that it be rotated every 30 days without a code change or redeployment.
scenarios.question: What should the team use?

options.text: AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation, retrieved at runtime
options.why: Rotation with no code change is precisely what Secrets Manager adds over the alternatives — it rotates the RDS credential and the function fetches the current value.

options.text: Systems Manager Parameter Store SecureString
options.why: Encrypts the value and is free for standard parameters, but it does not rotate a database credential for you. The 30-day requirement is the deciding factor.

options.text: A Lambda environment variable encrypted with a KMS key
options.why: Protects the value at rest, but changing it still means updating and redeploying the function.

options.text: Hard-code the password and restrict who can view the function
options.why: Puts a live credential in source control, where it will outlive both the restriction and the people who set it.

scenarios.situation: An application stores events in DynamoDB using the current date as the partition key. During busy periods writes are throttled even though provisioned capacity is well above the total write rate.
scenarios.question: What is the cause?

options.text: All writes for a given day share one partition key, creating a hot partition
options.why: Capacity is spread across partitions, not pooled. Every write on a given day targets one key, so that partition throttles while the rest of the table sits idle.

options.text: Provisioned capacity is set too low for the peak
options.why: The question states total capacity comfortably exceeds the write rate. Adding more would not fix an uneven distribution.

options.text: The table needs a global secondary index on the timestamp
options.why: Indexes change query options. They do not redistribute writes on the base table.

options.text: On-demand mode is required for this access pattern
options.why: On-demand adapts to overall volume but still partitions by key, so a single hot key can still throttle.

scenarios.situation: An organisation must guarantee that no workload in any member account can create resources outside two approved Regions — including by an account administrator with full IAM permissions.
scenarios.question: Which control achieves this?

options.text: A service control policy on the organizational unit denying actions outside those Regions
options.why: An SCP sets the ceiling on what an account can do at all. Even a full administrator cannot exceed it, which is the "including administrators" part of the requirement.

options.text: An IAM policy attached to every role denying other Regions
options.why: An administrator can edit or detach an IAM policy in their own account. It constrains users, not the account itself.

options.text: An AWS Config rule flagging resources in other Regions
options.why: Detects afterwards. The requirement is prevention.

options.text: A permissions boundary on each IAM role
options.why: Caps what a role can do and is useful for delegation, but an account administrator can alter boundaries within their account.

scenarios.situation: A company has 80 VPCs across several accounts that all need to reach a shared services VPC and an on-premises data centre. The current design uses VPC peering and has become unmanageable.
scenarios.question: What should the architect move to?

options.text: AWS Transit Gateway with one attachment per VPC, shared through Resource Access Manager
options.why: Each VPC attaches once to a hub instead of peering with every other, replacing an n-squared mesh with 80 attachments, and RAM shares the gateway across accounts.

options.text: A full mesh of VPC peering connections
options.why: That is the current design. Eighty VPCs need over three thousand peering connections, and peering is not transitive.

options.text: AWS PrivateLink endpoints between every pair of VPCs
options.why: PrivateLink exposes an individual service, not general network reachability, and per-pair endpoints scale no better than peering.

options.text: A VPN connection from each VPC to the data centre
options.why: Solves on-premises connectivity only, leaves VPC-to-VPC unsolved, and adds 80 tunnels to operate.

scenarios.situation: A team must transform 200 GB of nightly CSV exports into partitioned Parquet and register the result in a catalogue. Nobody on the team wants to manage clusters, and the job runs once a day.
scenarios.question: Which service fits best?

options.text: AWS Glue ETL jobs
options.why: Serverless Spark with a built-in catalogue, billed per DPU-hour only while the job runs. Nightly batch with no cluster to manage is exactly its shape.

options.text: Amazon EMR on EC2
options.why: Capable of the transform, but it provisions a cluster you size, tune and pay for. Overhead the team explicitly does not want for one nightly job.

options.text: AWS Lambda
options.why: The 15-minute timeout and memory ceiling make 200 GB of Spark-style transformation impractical.

options.text: Amazon Athena CTAS queries
options.why: Can write Parquet, but it is a query service — orchestration, retries and job bookmarks for a nightly pipeline are Glue’s job.

scenarios.situation: Clickstream events must feed three independent consumers: a real-time dashboard, a fraud model, and an archive in S3. One consumer occasionally fails and must be able to re-read the last 24 hours from where it stopped.
scenarios.question: Which ingestion service meets the requirement?

options.text: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
options.why: Records persist for a retention period and each consumer tracks its own position, so a failed consumer can replay without affecting the others.

options.text: Amazon Data Firehose
options.why: Delivers to a destination and forgets. There is nothing to re-read, and it cannot fan out to three independent consumers with separate positions.

options.text: Amazon SQS standard queue
options.why: A message is consumed once and deleted. Three consumers would each need their own queue, and there is no replay of processed messages.

options.text: Amazon SNS topic
options.why: Fans out to three subscribers, but stores nothing — a consumer that is down simply misses the messages.

scenarios.situation: Finance runs complex multi-table joins across five years of history for monthly reporting. Queries are heavy, run by a handful of analysts, and are expected to complete in seconds rather than minutes.
scenarios.question: Which service should hold this data?

options.text: Amazon Redshift
options.why: A columnar warehouse built for exactly this: large analytical joins and aggregations with fast, repeatable performance for a small analyst population.

options.text: Amazon Athena over S3
options.why: Excellent for ad-hoc querying with no infrastructure, but repeated heavy joins over five years scan a great deal of data and are slower and costlier than a warehouse.

options.text: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL
options.why: A row-store built for transactions. Five years of analytical joins is the workload it is worst at.

options.text: Amazon DynamoDB
options.why: Key-value lookups at scale. It cannot perform multi-table analytical joins at all.

scenarios.situation: Analysts must query a customer table in the data lake, but must not see the email or national insurance columns. Data scientists in a different team need full access to the same table.
scenarios.question: How should this be implemented?

options.text: AWS Lake Formation permissions granting column-level access per principal
options.why: Lake Formation enforces table, column and row level permissions at query time, so both teams read one table and see different columns.

options.text: Two copies of the table, one with the sensitive columns removed
options.why: Works but doubles storage, and the redacted copy drifts out of date the moment the source changes.

options.text: An S3 bucket policy denying the analysts access
options.why: Bucket policies operate on objects. They cannot express "this column but not that one" inside a file.

options.text: IAM policies on the Glue Data Catalog
options.why: Can control access to table metadata, but not to individual columns within the data.

scenarios.situation: A data lake holds raw event files. The last 30 days are queried constantly, the next 11 months occasionally, and anything older is kept only for a seven-year regulatory retention period and is essentially never read.
scenarios.question: What is the most cost-effective storage arrangement?

options.text: A lifecycle policy: Standard, then Standard-IA at 30 days, then Glacier Deep Archive at 12 months
options.why: Each tier matches the access pattern described, and the lifecycle policy performs the transitions automatically as objects age.

options.text: Keep everything in S3 Standard
options.why: Simplest, but pays hot-storage rates for seven years of data that nobody reads.

options.text: Move everything to Glacier Deep Archive immediately
options.why: Cheapest storage, but the last 30 days are queried constantly and Deep Archive retrieval takes hours.

options.text: Use S3 One Zone-IA for the archive tier
options.why: Cheaper than Standard-IA, but a single-AZ loss destroys the data — unacceptable for a regulatory retention copy.

scenarios.situation: An upstream team adds a column to the JSON files they deliver each night. Downstream Athena queries start failing because the catalogue no longer matches the files.
scenarios.question: What is the appropriate fix?

options.text: Schedule a Glue crawler to update the table schema as files change
options.why: Crawlers infer schema from the data and update the catalogue, which is precisely the mismatch described.

options.text: Ask the upstream team to stop changing the format
options.why: Schema evolution is normal in a data lake. A pipeline that cannot absorb it will keep breaking.

options.text: Recreate the Athena table manually after each change
options.why: Works once, but it is unscheduled manual toil that will be forgotten.

options.text: Convert the files to CSV
options.why: Changes the format without addressing the fact that the catalogue is not being updated.

scenarios.situation: A nightly pipeline has five stages. If stage three fails it should retry twice, then alert an on-call topic and stop rather than running stages four and five on incomplete data.
scenarios.question: How should the pipeline be built?

options.text: AWS Step Functions with per-state retry and catch, publishing to SNS on failure
options.why: Retry counts and failure branches are declared per state, and the run stops rather than continuing — with a visible execution history showing exactly which stage failed.

options.text: Chain the stages with S3 event notifications
options.why: Each stage triggers the next on success, but there is no retry policy, no failure branch and no single view of the run.

options.text: One large Lambda function running all five stages
options.why: Risks the 15-minute limit, and a failure at stage three restarts the whole thing from the beginning.

options.text: An EventBridge rule per stage on a cron schedule
options.why: Stages run on the clock regardless of whether the previous one succeeded — exactly the "incomplete data" problem to be avoided.

scenarios.situation: An operational DynamoDB table serves the live application. Analysts want to run large aggregate queries over the same data without risking the application’s latency.
scenarios.question: What should be done?

options.text: Stream changes to S3 and query there with Athena
options.why: Analytics runs against a copy in the data lake, so heavy scans never consume the table’s capacity or affect application latency.

options.text: Run the aggregate queries directly against the table with a Scan
options.why: A full Scan consumes read capacity across the table and is exactly what would degrade the live application.

options.text: Add a global secondary index for the analytics queries
options.why: Indexes serve known access patterns and still consume the table’s capacity. Ad-hoc aggregation is not what they are for.

options.text: Increase provisioned read capacity during business hours
options.why: Pays more to make the interference affordable rather than removing it.

scenarios.situation: A pipeline in a shared tooling account must deploy into separate development, staging and production accounts. Security requires no long-lived credentials for the target accounts.
scenarios.question: How should this be configured?

options.text: Cross-account IAM roles the pipeline assumes, with the artifact bucket and KMS key shared to the targets
options.why: Assuming a role yields temporary credentials per deployment, and the targets need access to the artifacts and the key that encrypted them.

options.text: Store each target account’s access keys in the pipeline as secrets
options.why: Long-lived credentials, which the requirement rules out — and rotating three sets by hand is how they end up stale.

options.text: Run a separate pipeline inside each target account
options.why: Triples the pipelines to maintain and loses the single promotion path from dev to production.

options.text: Give the tooling account’s role administrator access in each target
options.why: Solves the credential problem by discarding least privilege entirely.

scenarios.situation: A CloudFormation stack update fails halfway through, leaving some resources updated and others not. The team wants failed updates to leave the environment exactly as it was.
scenarios.question: What behaviour should they rely on and configure?

options.text: Automatic rollback on failure, verified beforehand with a change set
options.why: CloudFormation rolls a failed update back to the previous state by default, and a change set shows what the update would do before it is applied.

options.text: Delete and recreate the stack on every change
options.why: Guarantees consistency by destroying the environment and everything in it, including data.

options.text: Disable rollback so the team can inspect the failure
options.why: Useful occasionally for debugging, but it leaves exactly the half-updated state the team wants to avoid.

options.text: Use separate stacks per resource so failures are isolated
options.why: Fragments one deployment into many partial ones, making a consistent overall state harder, not easier.

scenarios.situation: Application logs from 25 accounts must land in one security account, be searchable, and be retained for two years. Individual account owners must not be able to delete them.
scenarios.question: Which design meets this?

options.text: Ship CloudWatch Logs to a central account and archive to a locked S3 bucket in that account
options.why: Ownership moves to the security account, so a member-account admin cannot delete the archive, and retention is enforced centrally.

options.text: Set a two-year retention on each account’s own log groups
options.why: The logs stay under the control of the account being audited, who can shorten retention or delete them.

options.text: Enable an organization CloudTrail trail
options.why: Correct for API activity, but the requirement is application logs, which CloudTrail does not capture.

options.text: Rely on the default CloudWatch Logs retention
options.why: The default is to keep logs indefinitely in the originating account — neither centralised nor tamper-resistant.

scenarios.situation: Security requires that any S3 bucket made public is returned to private within minutes, without waiting for a human.
scenarios.question: Which combination achieves this?

options.text: An AWS Config rule detecting public buckets with an automatic remediation action
options.why: Config continuously evaluates the rule and can trigger a Systems Manager Automation document to fix the finding without human involvement.

options.text: A weekly Trusted Advisor review
options.why: Detects the problem, but weekly is far outside "within minutes" and nothing is fixed automatically.

options.text: A service control policy denying public bucket configuration
options.why: A strong preventive control worth having, but the question asks for remediation of buckets that have already been changed.

options.text: A CloudWatch alarm on S3 request metrics
options.why: Request metrics say nothing about whether the bucket policy is public.

scenarios.situation: An ECS service behind an Application Load Balancer must be released so that the new task set can be validated on a test listener before any customer traffic reaches it.
scenarios.question: Which deployment approach provides this?

options.text: CodeDeploy blue/green deployment for ECS with a test listener
options.why: The replacement task set is registered to a separate test listener for validation, and production traffic only shifts once you are satisfied.

options.text: ECS rolling update with a minimum healthy percent of 100
options.why: Replaces tasks gradually and keeps capacity up, but every new task takes live traffic immediately — there is no pre-production validation step.

options.text: Stop the service and start it on the new task definition
options.why: Causes an outage, which the requirement rules out implicitly and common sense rules out explicitly.

options.text: Create a second ECS cluster and repoint DNS
options.why: A hand-rolled blue/green with DNS caching delays and no automated rollback.

scenarios.situation: When an EC2 instance fails its status check, the team wants an automated runbook to collect diagnostics and then reboot it, with a record of what ran.
scenarios.question: How should this be wired?

options.text: An EventBridge rule on the status-check event invoking a Systems Manager Automation runbook
options.why: EventBridge matches the event and Automation runs the documented steps, logging each execution for the record.

options.text: A CloudWatch alarm with an EC2 reboot action
options.why: Reboots the instance, but skips diagnostics entirely — and once rebooted the evidence is gone.

options.text: A cron job on a management instance polling the API
options.why: Introduces a server to maintain, adds polling delay, and fails when the management instance does.

options.text: An Auto Scaling health check replacing the instance
options.why: Replaces rather than investigates, which destroys the diagnostics the team asked to collect.

scenarios.situation: A build stage needs a third-party API token. It is currently a plaintext CodeBuild environment variable, visible to anyone who can view the project.
scenarios.question: What should replace it?

options.text: Store the token in Secrets Manager and reference it from the build environment
options.why: The value never appears in the project configuration or build logs, access is controlled by IAM, and it can be rotated centrally.

options.text: Encrypt the variable with a KMS key and keep it in the project
options.why: Better than plaintext, but the ciphertext still lives in project configuration and changing it means editing the project.

options.text: Commit the token to the repository in a config file
options.why: Puts a live credential into version history, where it survives every later deletion.

options.text: Pass the token as a build parameter at start time
options.why: Means a human types a secret on every build, and it lands in the build’s parameter record.

scenarios.situation: A team currently rebuilds the application separately for staging and production from the same commit. Occasionally the two builds differ because a dependency moved.
scenarios.question: What is the correct practice?

options.text: Build the artifact once and promote the same artifact through each environment
options.why: Building once removes the possibility of environment drift from a moving dependency — what you tested is byte-for-byte what you release.

options.text: Pin every dependency version and keep rebuilding per environment
options.why: Reduces the chance of drift but does not eliminate it, and still tests a different binary from the one released.

options.text: Rebuild but compare checksums before deploying
options.why: Detects the problem after wasting the build, and gives no path forward when they differ.

options.text: Deploy directly from the source repository to each environment
options.why: Removes the artifact entirely, so every environment resolves dependencies independently — the same problem, worse.

scenarios.situation: Instances in an Auto Scaling group must finish uploading their logs before they are terminated during a scale-in event. At present logs are lost when instances go away.
scenarios.question: What should be configured?

options.text: An Auto Scaling lifecycle hook on instance termination
options.why: The hook holds the instance in a wait state while the upload completes, then signals to continue — which is exactly the gap between "marked for termination" and "gone".

options.text: Termination protection on the instances
options.why: Prevents termination altogether, which breaks scale-in rather than sequencing it.

options.text: A longer health check grace period
options.why: Applies to instances starting up, not shutting down.

options.text: A CloudWatch alarm on the terminate event
options.why: Notifies after the fact. By then the instance and its logs are gone.

scenarios.situation: An operations team must guarantee daily backups of EBS volumes, RDS databases and EFS file systems, retained for 35 days, with one report proving compliance across all three.
scenarios.question: Which service provides this?

options.text: AWS Backup with a backup plan and vault
options.why: One policy covers all three services with a shared retention rule and produces compliance reporting — which per-service tooling cannot.

options.text: Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager
options.why: Handles EBS snapshots well, but does not cover RDS or EFS.

options.text: Automated RDS backups plus an EBS snapshot script
options.why: Covers two of the three with different mechanisms and no single compliance view.

options.text: S3 versioning on a backup bucket
options.why: Protects objects in a bucket. It backs up none of the three services named.

scenarios.situation: A web application runs in two Regions. If the primary Region becomes unhealthy, traffic should move to the secondary automatically, and return when the primary recovers.
scenarios.question: How should DNS be configured?

options.text: Route 53 failover routing with health checks on the primary endpoint
options.why: Health checks detect the failure and the failover policy answers with the secondary, reverting automatically once the primary passes again.

options.text: Route 53 weighted routing at 100/0
options.why: Sends all traffic to the primary, but nothing changes the weights when it fails — that would be a manual edit under pressure.

options.text: Route 53 simple routing with both addresses
options.why: Returns both addresses regardless of health, so half the users reach a dead endpoint.

options.text: Latency-based routing between the two Regions
options.why: Optimises for speed, not availability, and will keep sending nearby users to an unhealthy Region.

scenarios.situation: The team needs an alert when the application log contains more than ten "OutOfMemoryError" lines in five minutes. The string appears only in the log text, not in any metric.
scenarios.question: How is this achieved?

options.text: A CloudWatch Logs metric filter that emits a metric, with an alarm on it
options.why: Metric filters turn a matching log pattern into a numeric metric, which an alarm can then threshold — the standard bridge from log text to alerting.

options.text: A CloudWatch alarm directly on the log group
options.why: Alarms evaluate metrics, not raw log text. Something has to create the metric first.

options.text: CloudWatch Logs Insights query on a schedule
options.why: Good for investigation, but it is a query tool rather than an alerting mechanism.

options.text: EventBridge rule matching the log content
options.why: EventBridge matches events on the bus, not lines inside a log stream.

scenarios.situation: A regulator requires that a copy of audit objects exists in a second Region within 15 minutes of being written, and that the copy cannot be deleted by the source account’s administrators.
scenarios.question: What should be configured?

options.text: S3 Cross-Region Replication into a bucket in another account, with Object Lock enabled
options.why: Replication meets the time requirement, a different account removes the source administrators’ authority, and Object Lock makes the copy immutable.

options.text: S3 Cross-Region Replication into another bucket in the same account
options.why: Meets the timing and the Region, but the same administrators can still delete the copy.

options.text: A nightly batch copy with the AWS CLI
options.why: Up to 24 hours behind, well outside the 15-minute requirement.

options.text: S3 versioning on the source bucket
options.why: A prerequisite for replication, but on its own it keeps everything in one Region and one account.

scenarios.situation: A deployment fails with an error stating that the maximum number of VPCs in the Region has been reached. The team needs more.
scenarios.question: What is the correct response?

options.text: Request a quota increase through Service Quotas
options.why: Most quotas are soft limits raised on request. Service Quotas is the supported route, and the increase is per account and Region.

options.text: Deploy into a different Region
options.why: Sidesteps the limit but scatters the architecture for an administrative reason, and the same limit applies there.

options.text: Delete unused resources of a different type
options.why: Frees nothing against the VPC quota specifically.

options.text: Create a new AWS account for the extra VPCs
options.why: A legitimate pattern at scale, but a heavy answer when the quota can simply be raised.

scenarios.situation: During a Multi-AZ failover test, the application loses its database connection and does not recover until it is restarted. The database itself failed over successfully in about 90 seconds.
scenarios.question: What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The application caches the resolved IP address instead of honouring the DNS TTL
options.why: Failover repoints the RDS endpoint in DNS. An application holding the old address keeps dialling the failed instance until something forces it to resolve again.

options.text: Multi-AZ failover requires a manual restart of clients
options.why: It does not. The endpoint is designed so correctly behaving clients reconnect on their own.

options.text: The standby was in a different Region
options.why: Multi-AZ standbys are in the same Region by definition; cross-Region would be a read replica.

options.text: The security group blocked the standby
options.why: The security group is attached to the DB instance and follows the failover — it does not distinguish primary from standby.

scenarios.situation: A company with 40 accounts under Organizations needs to bill each internal business unit for the AWS resources it consumes, including shared services.
scenarios.question: What is the foundation of this?

options.text: A consistent tagging policy with cost allocation tags activated in the billing console
options.why: Tags are what let Cost Explorer and the Cost and Usage Report attribute spend by owner. Activation is the step people forget, and tags only apply from that point forward.

options.text: One AWS account per business unit and nothing else
options.why: Attributes most spend cleanly, but shared services still need tagging to split, and account-per-team does not scale to every project.

options.text: AWS Budgets per business unit
options.why: Alerts against a threshold. It cannot attribute existing spend to an owner.

options.text: Reading the consolidated invoice each month
options.why: Shows the total by service, not by internal owner.

scenarios.situation: A company must vacate its data centre in six months. One application is a commercial CRM with a SaaS equivalent, one is a legacy Windows app nobody understands, and one is a modern containerised service.
scenarios.question: Which strategies fit, in that order?

options.text: Repurchase the CRM, rehost the legacy app, replatform or relocate the container service
options.why: Each matches its constraints: a SaaS equivalent exists, the legacy app cannot be safely changed under a deadline, and the modern service moves with little effort.

options.text: Refactor all three for cloud-native architecture
options.why: Refactoring an unknown legacy application inside six months is how deadlines are missed.

options.text: Rehost all three unchanged
options.why: Safe but wasteful: it pays to keep running a CRM that could be replaced by SaaS, and ignores the container service’s portability.

options.text: Retain the legacy app on-premises
options.why: The data centre is closing. There is nowhere to retain it.

scenarios.situation: Instances in AWS must resolve names in an on-premises Active Directory zone, and on-premises servers must resolve private Route 53 zone names in AWS. A Direct Connect link is already in place.
scenarios.question: What should be deployed?

options.text: Route 53 Resolver inbound and outbound endpoints with forwarding rules
options.why: Outbound endpoints forward AWS queries to the on-premises resolvers; inbound endpoints let on-premises query AWS private zones. Both directions is why both endpoint types are needed.

options.text: A private hosted zone associated with the VPC
options.why: Resolves AWS names inside the VPC, but does nothing for on-premises zones in either direction.

options.text: Conditional forwarders on the on-premises DNS only
options.why: Solves one direction. AWS instances still cannot resolve the on-premises zone.

options.text: A public hosted zone for the internal names
options.why: Publishes internal names to the internet, which is a disclosure problem rather than a solution.

scenarios.situation: A company relies on a single Direct Connect connection for a critical hybrid workload. An audit flags it as a single point of failure, and the budget will not stretch to a second dedicated connection immediately.
scenarios.question: What is the pragmatic interim step?

options.text: Add a Site-to-Site VPN over the internet as a backup path
options.why: Far cheaper and quick to provision, giving a genuine second path with reduced performance rather than none at all when the circuit drops.

options.text: Accept the risk and document it
options.why: Documents rather than mitigates, when a cheap mitigation exists.

options.text: Increase the bandwidth of the existing connection
options.why: More capacity on the same physical path. A cut cable takes it all out regardless.

options.text: Move the workload fully into AWS
options.why: May be the eventual answer, but it is a large programme rather than an interim resilience step.
